power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p's ≤ 0.011", Text = "Both pTau217/Aβ42 and pTau217 were significantly higher in Aβ+ participants compared with Aβ-participants, across all diagnostic groups (all p's ≤ 0.011; Figure 1C and 1D)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

table.expanded: Next, pTau217/Aβ42 performed comparably in CeVD-and CeVD+ individuals, demonstrating good performance in both groups (AUC [95% CI]; CeVD-: 0.967 [0.906-1.00]; CeVD+: 0.940 [0.898-0.983]; p = 0.48).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.48", Sentence = "Next, pTau217/Aβ42 performed comparably in CeVD-and CeVD+ individuals, demonstrating good performance in both groups (AUC [95% CI]; CeVD-: 0.967 [0.906-1.00]; CeVD+: 0.940 [0.898-0.983]; p = 0.48)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: The generalizability of FDA-cleared Lumipulse plasma pTau217 / Aβ42 ratio cutpoints to Asian populations remains uncertain, especially in those with high burden of concomitant cerebrovascular disease (CeVD).
We evaluated pTau217, Aβ42 and their ratio in 205 Singapore-based participants with corresponding amyloid neuroimaging.
Inhouse cutpoints were derived using a three-range strategy targeting 95% sensitivity and specificity.
Plasma pTau217/Aβ42 ratio outperformed pTau217 alone (area under the curve, 0.951 versus 0.925; p=0.004), with comparable performance across CeVD severities.
Plasma ratio cutpoints achieved 98% negative predictive value, 88% positive predictive value, and 95% accuracy, classifying 10% as intermediate-risk.

Using FDAcleared cutpoints for our cohort retained 97% sensitivity and negative predictive value but yielded lower specificity (86%), positive predictive value (77%) and accuracy (85%), with 29% classified as intermediate-risk.
Our findings support the need for populationspecific validation of cutpoints from FDA-cleared blood biomarkers of brain amyloid pathology.

The Lumipulse G pTau217/Aβ42 plasma ratio from Fujirebio (Tokyo, Japan) is the first US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared blood-based marker of amyloid pathology associated with Alzheimer's disease in symptomatic older adults [1].
text.formatted: The Lumipulse G pTau217/Aβ42 plasma ratio from Fujirebio (Tokyo, Japan) is the first US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared blood-based marker of amyloid pathology associated with Alzheimer's disease in symptomatic older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Although the FDA-reviewed multi-center study reported good diagnostic performance of the published cutpoints [2], an important caveat remains: the cohort was predominantly White (85%), and the generalizability of these cutpoints to non-White populations remains under-studied, particularly amongst individuals with differing sociodemographic characteristics and comorbidities that may influence plasma biomarker profiles [3] [4] [5].
text.formatted: Although the FDA-reviewed multi-center study reported good diagnostic performance of the published cutpoints <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>, an important caveat remains: the cohort was predominantly White (85%), and the generalizability of these cutpoints to non-White populations remains under-studied, particularly amongst individuals with differing sociodemographic characteristics and comorbidities that may influence plasma biomarker profiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Here, using a well characterized, longitudinally assessed Asian cohort with high concomitant cerebrovascular disease (CeVD) burden and vascular risk factors [6], we evaluated Lumipulse pTau217/Aβ42 plasma ratio and pTau217 alone for detection of amyloid positivity (Aβ+) on positron emission tomography (PET), derived in-house cutpoints using a three-range strategy, and compared their performance with FDAcleared cutpoints.

text.text: Briefly, Images scanned with [ 11 C]-Pittsburgh Compound B (PiB) or [ 18 F]-flutafuranol on an mMR synchronous PET/MR scanner (Siemens Healthcare GmbH, Munich, Germany) were reconstructed using ordinary Poisson ordered-subsets expectation maximization with all corrections applied, with each image visually interpreted independently as Aβ+ or Aβ-by three experienced raters blinded to the clinical diagnosis of participants.

Blood from non-fasted participants was collected into ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) tubes and centrifuged at 2000 g for 10 minutes at 4•C. Plasma was extracted, aliquoted and stored at -80•C until use.

The chemiluminescent enzyme immunoassaybased Lumipulse® G assays for plasma pTau217 (tau phosphorylated at threonine 217) and Aβ42 (recognizing β-amyloid 1-42 peptide) were performed by Fujirebio Diagnostics Inc.'s subsidiary in Tokyo, Japan (reagent lots: D4C6086J and C5C6091S) and expressed in units of pg/mL.
Evaluators were blinded to clinical information.  1 and Figure 1A, 1B.
text.formatted: Evaluators were blinded to clinical information.  <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">1A</ref>, 1B.

text.text: Results 205 participants were included (mean [SD] age, 75.7 [6.9] years; 118 [58%] female; 43 cognitively normal [CN], 98 cognitively impaired no dementia [CIND], 64 dementia; 67 were PET Aβ+ [33%]; 145 had significant CeVD [73%]; see Supplementary Table 1).
Both pTau217/Aβ42 and pTau217 were significantly higher in Aβ+ participants compared with Aβ-participants, across all diagnostic groups (all p's ≤ 0.011; Figure 1C and 1D).
text.formatted: Both pTau217/Aβ42 and pTau217 were significantly higher in Aβ+ participants compared with Aβ-participants, across all diagnostic groups (all p's ≤ 0.011; Figure <ref type="figure">1C</ref> and 1D).

text.text: Compared with pTau217, pTau217/Aβ42 showed higher percentage increase between Aβand Aβ+ participants in all clinical stages.
Plasma pTau217/Aβ42 (AUC [95% CI] = 0.951 [0.917-0.985]) outperformed pTau217 alone (AUC [95% CI] = 0.925 [0.881-0.968]) in detecting PET Aβ+ (p = 0.004).

In sensitivity analyses, among dementia-free participants (CN + CIND), pTau217/Aβ42 also achieved a high AUC of 0.936 (95% CI, 0.883-0.990), outperforming pTau217 (AUC [95% CI] = 0.911 [0.844-0.978]; p = 0.035).
Next, pTau217/Aβ42 performed comparably in CeVD-and CeVD+ individuals, demonstrating good performance in both groups (AUC [95% CI]; CeVD-: 0.967 [0.906-1.00]; CeVD+: 0.940 [0.898-0.983]; p = 0.48).

Using in-house pTau217/Aβ42 cutpoints (95% sensitivity, 95% specificity), lowand high-risk classifications achieved negative predictive value (NPV) of 98%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 88%, and accuracy of 95% (Table 1).
text.formatted: Using in-house pTau217/Aβ42 cutpoints (95% sensitivity, 95% specificity), lowand high-risk classifications achieved negative predictive value (NPV) of 98%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 88%, and accuracy of 95% (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The proportion of participants in intermediate-risk group was 10%.
Using FDA-cleared pTau217/Aβ42 cutpoints, sensitivity and NPV remained high at 97%.
However, specificity decreased to 86%, PPV to 77%, and accuracy to 85%.
Additionally, the proportion with intermediateor indeterminate risk was substantially higher at 29%.
In-house pTau217 cutpoints yielded NPV, PPV, and accuracy of 97%, 87%, and 94%, respectively, with 24% of participants in intermediate-risk group.

To identify potential factors associated with discrepancies between classifications based on FDA-cleared and in-house cutpoints, we compared demographic and comorbidity profiles of participants with concordant versus discordant risk group classifications.

The discordant group had a lower proportion of females (38% vs 72%; p < 0.001 by chi-square test) and higher proportions of participants with diabetes (35% vs 23%; p = 0.048) and chronic kidney disease (76% vs 61%; p = 0.025).
text.formatted: The discordant group had a lower proportion of females (38% vs 72%; p < 0.001 by chi-square test) and higher proportions of participants with diabetes (35% vs 23%; p = 0.048) and chronic kidney disease (76% vs 61%; p = 0.025).

text.text: With the advent of ultrasensitive platforms, the field of dementia blood-based biomarkers research is advancing rapidly, currently reaching a consensus that plasma phosphorylated tau species are associated with brain amyloid burden, with pTau217 generally demonstrating higher accuracy for detecting amyloid pathology compared to other pTau species [11, 12].
text.formatted: With the advent of ultrasensitive platforms, the field of dementia blood-based biomarkers research is advancing rapidly, currently reaching a consensus that plasma phosphorylated tau species are associated with brain amyloid burden, with pTau217 generally demonstrating higher accuracy for detecting amyloid pathology compared to other pTau species <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>.

text.text: This consensus is reflected by three out of four of the recommended that for a blood-based biomarker test to be useful in the clinical setting for amyloid pathology risk-stratification, the proportion of intermediate-risk in threerange cutoffs should be no more than 15-20% in a typical clinical population [13].
text.formatted: This consensus is reflected by three out of four of the recommended that for a blood-based biomarker test to be useful in the clinical setting for amyloid pathology risk-stratification, the proportion of intermediate-risk in threerange cutoffs should be no more than 15-20% in a typical clinical population <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: In our cohort, using the in-house cutpoints met the recommended threshold, whilst using FDAcleared cutpoints did not.
There is further evidence of cohort differences from the few other non-White studies published for the Lumipulse assay.
For example, similar to our findings, a Japanese study reported decreases of intermediate-risk proportions when locally optimized thresholds were used instead of the FDA-cleared cutpoints [14].
text.formatted: For example, similar to our findings, a Japanese study reported decreases of intermediate-risk proportions when locally optimized thresholds were used instead of the FDA-cleared cutpoints <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, a head-to-head comparison of Black / African American vs.
White participants showed high and comparable performance across the two races [15].
text.formatted: White participants showed high and comparable performance across the two races <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings underscore the importance of validating biomarker performance and cutpoints, as well as comparisons with FDA-cleared cutpoints, in cohorts that resemble the intended-use populations as blood biomarkers enter routine clinical practice.

Furthermore, as newer biomarkers (e.g., brain-derived pTau and eMTBR-tau243 [10, 16, 17]) enter evaluation phases, it may be worthwhile to diversify the cohorts under validation both ethnically and geographically.
text.formatted: Furthermore, as newer biomarkers (e.g., brain-derived pTau and eMTBR-tau243 <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref>) enter evaluation phases, it may be worthwhile to diversify the cohorts under validation both ethnically and geographically.

text.text: Finally, given the single-cohort design of this study, further validation is warranted in other Asian cohorts and under-represented populations, where differences in demographic characteristics and comorbidity profiles, or preanalytical and analytical factors [18], may influence the performance and applicability of blood biomarkers and their cutpoints [5].

Differences in plasma biomarkers among groups stratified by clinical diagnosis and Aβ-PET status were assessed using Kruskal-Wallis analyses of variance and post-hoc Dunn's tests.
Diagnostic performance for detecting PET Aβ+ was assessed using area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUC).
P-values for comparison of AUCs were derived from DeLong tests.

In-house pTau217/Aβ42 and pTau217 cutpoints for PET Aβ+ were derived using a three-range strategy comprising a lower reference point to rule out AD (95% sensitivity; low-risk for PET Aβ+) and a higher reference point to rule in AD (95% specificity; high-risk for PET Aβ+).
Participants with values between the reference points were classified as having intermediate-risk.

All in-house and FDAcleared cutpoints are presented in Table currently FDA-cleared blood tests incorporating pTau217, either by itself (Elecys pTau217 from Roche), or combined with Aβ (PrecivityAD2 from C2N Diagnostic as well as Lumipulse).
As the first FDA-cleared blood test, the Lumipulse plasma pTau217/Aβ42 ratio has had some lead time for characterization, but the majority of studies remain focused on western populations.

Here, we have demonstrated excellent performance of the Lumipulse plasma pTau217/Aβ42 ratio in detecting abnormal brain amyloid burden in an Asian cohort with high prevalence of concomitant CeVD (AUC = 0.951).

While both in-house and FDA-cleared pTau217/Aβ42 cutpoints achieved high NPV and sensitivity of ≥ 95%, the in-house cutpoints outperformed FDA-cleared cutpoints by reducing the proportion of intermediate-risk results (29% vs. 10%) and improving PPV, specificity, and accuracy.
